title: Is Money the Root of All Evil?
excerpt: The Bible never says that money is the root of all evil. It says something harder: that the love of it is a root of many evils, in the poor as well as the rich, and that the first people Paul had in mind were religious teachers.
body:
A man who built a plumbing company from one van to forty has sat through enough sermons to conclude that his church regards what he does all week as slightly dirty. It accepts his checks, and it has never once asked him what it is like to make a payroll. A couple three rows back are carrying a hospital bill, two credit cards and a car loan, and every sermon on giving leaves them feeling condemned twice, once for owing and once for not tithing. A widow mailed part of her pension each month for six years to a preacher on television who promised that God would return it many times over. Nothing came back, and she has begun to wonder what was wrong with her faith.

The skeptic has watched the offering plate go by and has a question of his own. The church says that money is the root of all evil, he points out, and then asks for some.

The sentence he is quoting is not in the Bible. What the Bible does say is harder on the businessman, the couple, the widow's preacher and the skeptic alike.

## What the Verse Says

The line comes from Paul's first letter to Timothy, and in the old English Bible that most people half remember it reads, "the love of money is the root of all evil." Even in that form the subject is love. Money, the thing itself, is not accused. A more recent translation reads, "For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils" (1 Timothy 6:10). On that rendering it is one root, among others, of many kinds of evil. Either way, Paul is not offering a theory that every sin in the world goes back to cash. Cain did not kill Abel for money, and David did not take Bathsheba for it.

The setting narrows the sentence further. Paul has just described teachers who were "imagining that godliness is a means of gain" (1 Timothy 6:5), men who had found that religion could be made to pay. Against them he sets a different kind of profit: "godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world" (1 Timothy 6:6–7). Then he says where the danger lies, and he locates it in a desire: "those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare" (1 Timothy 6:9). He finishes the verse everyone half remembers with a report of casualties. "It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs" (1 Timothy 6:10).

Two things follow from reading it whole. The warning is aimed at wanting, and a person can want money desperately without having any. Paul's sentence about craving describes the poor man who thinks of nothing else as exactly as it describes the rich man who can never have enough. And the first people the passage has in view are religious teachers. The verse was written about the pulpit before it was written about the bank.

A few lines later Paul speaks to believers who were in fact rich, and he does not tell them to stop being so. He tells them "not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy," and "to be generous and ready to share" (1 Timothy 6:17–18). Enjoyment is in that sentence, beside the warning.

## A Tool and a Rival

Scripture treats money in two ways that have to be kept together.

It is a tool, and often a good one. Moses told Israel that it is God "who gives you power to get wealth" (Deuteronomy 8:18). With money a field is bought, a worker is paid, a child is fed, a traveler beaten on the road is put up at an inn at a stranger's expense. The Bible has no romance about being without it.

It is also the one created thing Jesus named as a rival to God. "No one can serve two masters," he said. "You cannot serve God and money" (Matthew 6:24). Money makes promises that few other things can. It offers safety and standing, and the freedom to need no one, and those are the things people have always asked of a god. "He who loves money will not be satisfied with money" (Ecclesiastes 5:10), which is what one would expect of an idol.

Jesus' two best-known meetings with rich men go in opposite directions, and the difference is instructive. One man was told, "go, sell all that you have and give to the poor," and "he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions" (Mark 10:21–22). The other was a tax collector named Zacchaeus, who was asked for nothing. He stood up at his own table and said, "the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold," and Jesus answered, "Today salvation has come to this house" (Luke 19:8–9). One man kept everything and lost the thing he came for. The other kept what was left after his repayments and was left in peace with it. Jesus did not hand the two men a single rule. In each case he went after whatever had hold of the man. The question of how much a Christian may keep has divided the church since its early centuries, and another essay on this site, on [whether a Christian can be rich](/writing/can-a-christian-be-rich), follows that argument.

## What the First Christians Did

The earliest churches drew a practical conclusion, and outsiders noticed it.

In Jerusalem "all who believed were together and had all things in common. And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need" (Acts 2:44–45). When Paul organized a collection among his Gentile churches for the poor in Judea, he described its aim with a word seldom heard in fundraising: "as a matter of fairness your abundance at the present time should supply their need" (2 Corinthians 8:13–14). An early manual of church life, the Didache, puts it as a command: "thou shalt share all things with thy brother, and shalt not say that they are thine own."

The clearest picture comes from the middle of the second century, in Justin's account of a Sunday service written for the emperor. After the reading, the sermon and the meal, he says, "they who are well to do, and willing, give what each thinks fit; and what is collected is deposited with the president, who succours the orphans and widows." Around the year 200 Tertullian described the same chest in North Africa and insisted on the same freedom: "there is no compulsion; all is voluntary." The money went, he said, "to support and bury poor people," to orphans, to the old, to the shipwrecked and to prisoners. "One in mind and soul, we do not hesitate to share our earthly goods with one another."

Three features of that record are worth holding on to. The giving was free, and the writers took care to say so. It was aimed at need, by name: widows, orphans, the sick, prisoners, strangers. And nobody in these accounts gave in order to get. The first Christians did not despise money. They moved it, on purpose, toward people who had none.

## The Promise of Return

That is the measure against which the teaching the widow trusted has to be set. This site's history course describes it as "a faith that reads divine favor in health and wealth." Its promise is simple. Believe and give, and God will make you prosper, and the gift that counts most is the one sent to the preacher.

The people who believe it should be understood before they are corrected. Many of them are poor, and they have been told, truly, that God cares whether the rent is paid, which is more than some comfortable churches have managed to say to them. But the teaching itself is the thing Paul described in the sentence before his warning: godliness treated as a means of gain. It makes God the instrument and money the goal. And when the harvest does not come, it lays the blame on the faith of the person who gave. The widow's faith was not the problem. She was sold something, in God's name, by people who profited from the sale, and the rest of us let it go on for decades without much protest. That should be said with grief and without contempt for her.

## Work, Provision and the Opposite Error

There is a mistake on the other side, and it is common among people who are proud of having avoided the first one. It treats money as unclean and the earning of it as a lower calling.

The New Testament gives no support to that. "If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat," Paul told one church, and he ordered the idle "to do their work quietly and to earn their own living" (2 Thessalonians 3:10, 12). He wrote to Timothy, a chapter before the famous verse, that anyone who "does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household," has "denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever" (1 Timothy 5:8). And in one sentence he gave honest work its purpose: the former thief is to labor "with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need" (Ephesians 4:28). In that sentence work earns the money, and the money is given.

So the man with forty vans is not doing something the church should merely tolerate. Wages paid on time feed families. A spirituality that looks down on him, while living on what he and people like him put in the plate, has not thought very hard about where its own bread comes from. Contempt for money is often a luxury of those who have never had to raise it. It can also hide a refusal to carry one's own weight, with the bills left for someone else to pay.

## Debt

The couple three rows back need more care than a slogan. What follows is what Scripture says, set down as plainly as possible. It is not financial advice, and anyone in serious debt should talk with someone qualified to give it. The site's page for people under this weight, [Money is a weight on me](/help/money), starts in the right place: "You don't have to fix it tonight. Tonight, just write down what's due this week and tell one person the truth."

The Bible speaks of debt as a danger and never calls a debtor a sinner simply for owing. "The borrower is the slave of the lender" (Proverbs 22:7) is an observation about power, and anyone who has owed money knows it is accurate. "Owe no one anything, except to love each other" (Romans 13:8) tells Christians to pay what is due. Neither verse was written to shame people who borrowed because someone was sick.

The law of Moses is far more concerned with lenders. "If you lend money to any of my people with you who is poor, you shall not be like a moneylender to him, and you shall not exact interest from him" (Exodus 22:25). A cloak taken as security had to be returned by nightfall, because the man needed it to sleep in. Every seventh year debts were to be released. When the nobles of Jerusalem were found charging interest to their own hungry neighbors and taking their fields, Nehemiah confronted them in public: "Let us abandon this exacting of interest" (Nehemiah 5:10). Jesus went past the law: "lend, expecting nothing in return" (Luke 6:35). And he put the word into the prayer he taught, where sinners ask God to "forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors" (Matthew 6:12).

For many centuries the church took those texts at their word and forbade lending at interest. Thomas Aquinas, in the thirteenth century, stated the old rule flatly: "To take usury for money lent is unjust in itself." Later Christians distinguished between a loan to a neighbor in need and a loan to a merchant for his business, and most churches came to accept interest of the second kind. That is a real disagreement about how an ancient law applies to a modern economy, and it is not settled here. What does not change is whose side the Bible takes when a lender grows rich on the desperation of the poor.

Two errors follow. One is to treat every debtor as a failure, and it falls hardest on people who were forced to borrow. The other is to treat borrowing as a normal way to live above one's income, which is the love of money on an installment plan.

## Generosity and Enough

Paul's alternative to the craving has two parts, and both are in the passage where this essay began.

The first is contentment. "If we have food and clothing, with these we will be content" (1 Timothy 6:8). He claimed elsewhere to have "learned the secret of facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need" (Philippians 4:12), and it had to be learned. The Stoic philosophers of his day praised the same quality and found its source in the self. The Study Bible's note on the chapter marks the difference: for Paul, "contentment rests not in the self but in God." It is why Jesus taught his followers to ask for bread a day at a time.

The second is giving, and Paul's rule for it leaves out both the pressure and the percentage. "Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7). Churches differ on whether the tenth that Israel gave is a rule for Christians, a place to start, or a guide, and this essay does not decide the matter. What the New Testament measures is cost. Jesus watched the rich put large sums into the temple treasury and said that a widow with two small coins had "put in more than all" of them, because they gave "out of their abundance" and she gave "all she had to live on" (Mark 12:43–44).

## What We Have Done

The church's own record with money is the best argument the skeptic has.

We have preached on giving and been silent about greed, because the people who give most are often the people a sermon on greed would be about. We have shamed debtors and courted donors. We have let the widow's preacher speak for us. And we have used guilt and pressure to raise money that Tertullian's church raised by saying there was no compulsion at all. The offering plate is not the scandal. The first Christians passed one, and it buried the poor. The scandal comes when the plate begins to serve the people who are passing it.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Money is not evil, and Scripture never says it is. The love of it is a root of many evils, and it grows in the poor and the rich. God's favor is not for sale, and a teaching that promises wealth in exchange for faith or for gifts has put something else in the place of the gospel. A Christian is to work, to provide for those who depend on him, to pay what he owes, to give freely and to care for the poor.

How much a believer may keep, whether the tithe binds, and what the old laws on interest require now are questions on which faithful Christians differ.

Paul ended his warning with a strange image. Those who chase wealth, he said, have "pierced themselves." Nobody did it to them. The businessman was told that money is dirty, the couple that owing is a disgrace, and the widow that giving is an investment. Each was told wrong, by people who should have known better.

The skeptic misquoted the verse, and so do most of us, and the misquotation is a comfort. If money were the root, a person could get clear of it by having less. Paul puts the root in a love, and a love cannot be left behind in an afternoon. It goes wherever its owner goes, into a small house as easily as a large one.

*"But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world."* (1 Timothy 6:6–7)

*"You cannot serve God and money."* (Matthew 6:24)
